title: Help
intro: A short guide to the main parts of this online judge.
aboutEmpty: The site has not configured an about page yet.

body.1: Any user can create a domain. A teacher can make one for a course and add problems and students to it; a team can use a domain as a shared space.
body.2: Roles and permissions decide whether a domain is public or private. Each domain has its own problem set, discussions, trainings and contests.
body.3: The default domain is system. Opening the main site address lands in this domain, and the logo returns to it from anywhere.

body.1: Time is measured as the CPU time the process uses. Unless a problem says otherwise, the limit is the one declared for each test case.
body.2: Memory is measured as the sum of the process's virtual and physical memory. The default is 256 MiB unless the problem declares a different per-case limit.

body.1: Unless stated otherwise, programs read from standard input and write to standard output.

Waiting, Fetched, Compiling and Judging mean the submission is still being processed. Accepted means the output matched. Wrong Answer means it did not, ignoring trailing whitespace at the end of a line and a final newline. Time or memory limit exceeded, runtime errors, compile errors and system errors are reported with their own names. Ignored or canceled submissions are not counted. A submission marked as canceled by an administrator may indicate a rule violation, such as code that closely matches another user's.
Common causes: the wrong language was selected; for Java the main class is not named Main; the code has a normal syntax or type error.
body.2: C and C++ notes: use long long instead of __int64, declare main as returning int, expect a loop variable declared in for to go out of scope afterwards, do not rely on itoa, and use %f rather than %lf with printf.

body.1: Curated problem sets are available under Training in the navigation. Open a training to see its chapters and your progress.

Each contest rule defines how submissions and the scoreboard work. Under IOI, XCPC and Ledo rules you may submit repeatedly and see results while the contest runs; under IOI, XCPC and Ledo you can also see the scoreboard during the contest.
body.2: Under OI rules only the last submission counts, so avoid a final compile error. Total score decides the ranking, and equal totals share a rank.
body.3: Under XCPC rules each wrong submission adds 20 minutes of penalty. The team that solves more problems ranks first; ties are broken by less total time including penalties.
body.4: Under Ledo rules repeated submissions reduce the score shown on the scoreboard, and the highest score counts. Each problem's final score is s times max(0.95^n, 0.7), where s is the score of this submission and n is the number of attempts before it.

body.1: RP is earned from problems, activities and contests. A user who has opted out of the leaderboard still earns RP; they are simply not listed in the ranking.
Difficulty is computed from submission counts, acceptance ratio and the timing and results of each submission.
body.2: Larger values mean harder problems. A new problem's difficulty can be inaccurate until it receives enough submissions, and early submissions weigh more in the calculation.

body.1: Markdown fields use CommonMark with extensions: KaTeX math, @[](/user/12) to mention a user, ==text== to highlight, image sizes with ![alt](url =100x100), @[video](url), @[bilibili](id), @[pdf](url), file://name to link an attachment of a problem, contest, homework or training, and a subset of HTML tags.
If something looks wrong or you want to report a post, start a discussion on the site or contact an administrator through the site's published contact details.
